steps.premise: The maker plans to return to trim a piece or add a handle.
steps.action: Have the maker clip handling instructions to the board.
steps.consequence: Classmates can tell whether they may uncover the piece.
steps.quote: Let people clip a handling note to their board when they're coming back to trim or attach a handle. A classmate can then tell whether it's okay to uncover the piece.

steps.premise: Some members struggle to lift a loaded board above their shoulders.
steps.action: Reserve space within easy reach for those members.
steps.consequence: They can use the rack without that lift.
steps.quote: Save some easy-reach space for anyone who would struggle to lift a loaded board above shoulder height.

steps.premise: A volunteer makes weekly rounds and needs to select owners for follow-up.
steps.action: Mark each board with the date it arrived.
steps.consequence: The volunteer can see whose work to ask about.
steps.quote: Date the arrival of each board so the volunteer doing the weekly round knows which owners to check in with.

steps.premise: A separately drying lid can be hard to distinguish from others later.
steps.action: Dry the lid and its matching piece on the same board.
steps.consequence: The maker can find the right lid at their next session.
steps.quote: For a project with a separate lid, keep the two parts together on one board while they dry. The maker won't have to hunt through similar lids at the next session.

steps.premise: Another person may spot damage while the piece can still be repaired.
steps.action: Give the person who sees it a way to notify the maker privately.
steps.consequence: The maker can decide in time whether to attempt a repair.
steps.quote: Give anyone who spots damage a way to leave the maker a private note. The owner can decide whether to repair the piece while there's still time.

steps.premise: A member's piece might need attention while they are away.
steps.action: Let the member designate someone to check their work.
steps.consequence: Staff know whom to ask about the piece during the absence.
steps.quote: Let members nominate someone to check their work during an absence, giving staff a known person to ask if a piece needs attention.

steps.premise: Whether a request can be filled depends on how many chairs remain on its date.
steps.action: Show each date's available chair count on the shared booking calendar.
steps.consequence: Organizers can tell whether enough chairs are available.
steps.quote: Put the number of available chairs against each date on a shared booking calendar so organizers can see whether a request will fit.

steps.premise: A late driver may need to reach the person with the keys during the event.
steps.action: Ask each organizer to identify an event contact who can be reached then.
steps.consequence: The driver knows whom to call about access.
steps.quote: Have each organizer name someone reachable during the event. A driver running late can call the person with the keys.

steps.premise: Borrowers need to judge how many chairs their vehicle can take.
steps.action: Publish the size of a folded chair and of a nested stack.
steps.consequence: Borrowers can check what will fit.
steps.quote: Publish the dimensions of a folded chair and a nested stack so a borrower can work out what will fit in their vehicle.

steps.premise: A chair with a loose hinge or a missing foot needs repair.
steps.action: Tag it visibly and store it apart from the other chairs.
steps.consequence: It stays out of the next delivery.
steps.quote: Give a chair with a loose hinge or missing foot a conspicuous repair tag and a separate storage spot, keeping it out of the next delivery.

steps.premise: Returned chairs need to be checked and cleaned before the next collection.
steps.action: Leave time between bookings for both jobs.
steps.consequence: The team can prepare the batch before the next group arrives.
steps.quote: Allow time between bookings to check and clean a returned batch before another group expects to collect it.

steps.premise: The organizer might have to leave the event early.
steps.action: Let the borrower choose someone else to return the chairs.
steps.consequence: The return can still happen on time.
steps.quote: Let a borrower nominate another person to make the return so the chairs can get back on time even when the event organizer has to leave early.

steps.premise: Visitors need to grasp captions at a glance.
steps.action: Put line breaks at natural pauses in the sentence and keep first and last names on one line.
steps.consequence: The wording and names are easier to read quickly.
steps.quote: Break lines at natural points in a sentence and keep a person's first and last name together to make the text easier to take in at a glance.

steps.premise: Visitors need to read the opening words as a session begins.
steps.action: Turn captions on at the start of each new session.
steps.consequence: Visitors can follow the opening immediately without looking for a setting.
steps.quote: Start a fresh listening session with captions visible so a visitor can read the opening words without searching through settings.

steps.premise: A listener relying on captions may find a reply hard to place.
steps.action: Have a reviewer follow the whole interview muted and mark replies that seem unprompted.
steps.consequence: The review identifies where the captions leave a reply unexplained.
steps.quote: Ask a reviewer to follow a complete interview with the sound muted and flag places where a reply seems to come out of nowhere.

steps.premise: Staff need to locate an error that a visitor reports.
steps.action: Provide a correction slip that asks for the interview title and the time in the recording.
steps.consequence: Staff can find the passage the visitor means.
steps.quote: Give visitors a correction slip with space for the interview title and playback time so staff can find a reported error.

steps.premise: A narrator may switch to reading someone else's letter or diary.
steps.action: Introduce the quoted material in the captions when the reading begins.
steps.consequence: Visitors know whose words the narrator is reading.
steps.quote: Introduce a recorded letter or diary excerpt in the captions when a narrator starts reading aloud, so visitors know whose words are being quoted.

steps.premise: People may join a looping exhibit partway through an interview.
steps.action: Keep the interview title alongside the captions.
steps.consequence: A newcomer can identify the story already playing.
steps.quote: For an exhibit that plays on a loop, display the interview title alongside the captions so someone arriving midway can place the story.

steps.premise: A beginner may forget a new figure during a song.
steps.action: Teach a basic step that works for the entire song.
steps.consequence: They have a familiar step to fall back on.
steps.quote: Give beginners a basic step they can use for a whole song, leaving them something dependable to return to when a new figure slips their mind.

steps.premise: Some pairs feel more confident practicing together.
steps.action: Make changes of partner optional during the lesson.
steps.consequence: Those pairs can stay together.
steps.quote: Make partner changes optional during the lesson so two people who feel steadier practicing together can keep their place.

steps.premise: A pair that falls out of time may miss the rest of a song.
steps.action: Teach partners to stop and find the beat again.
steps.consequence: They can resume dancing before the song ends.
steps.quote: Teach a pair how to stop and pick up the beat again. Losing time needn't cost them the rest of the song.

steps.premise: A new dancer may want to pause for water.
steps.action: Put drinking water in a visible, accessible place.
steps.consequence: They can take a break without finding the host.
steps.quote: Put drinking water somewhere easy to spot and reach, allowing a new dancer to take a break without having to track down the host.

steps.premise: Other couples may pass a beginner on a crowded floor.
steps.action: Show everyone which direction dancers travel.
steps.consequence: The new couple knows where to expect passing dancers.
steps.quote: Walk everyone through the direction of travel on a busy floor so a new couple knows where other dancers are likely to pass.

steps.premise: Guests practicing unfamiliar steps may encounter belongings on the floor.
steps.action: Set aside a place for coats and bags outside the dancing area.
steps.consequence: Guests can concentrate on their steps without dodging belongings.
steps.quote: Give bags and coats a home away from the dancing area. A guest concentrating on unfamiliar steps shouldn't have to weave around belongings.

steps.premise: Neighbors coming from work may arrive later in the advertised hours.
steps.action: With contributors' agreement, hold back some bread to put out later.
steps.consequence: Later arrivals still have a choice.
steps.quote: Save some bread from willing contributors for a later release during the advertised hours, so arriving straight from work still means finding a choice.

steps.premise: A participant may take home slices from several loaves.
steps.action: Supply paper bags that hold several slices and a pencil for labeling them.
steps.consequence: People can distinguish their selections at home.
steps.quote: Set out paper bags big enough for a few slices and a pencil for writing on them, so people can tell their selections apart once they're home.

steps.premise: Someone considering an unfamiliar loaf may be unsure how to enjoy it the next day.
steps.action: Ask its baker for a next-day serving tip, such as reheating or toasting.
steps.consequence: The advice can make the loaf easier to choose.
steps.quote: Ask each baker how they like to eat their bread the following day. A reheating or toasting suggestion makes a less familiar loaf easier to choose.

steps.premise: A neighbor may arrive without a contribution after their baking goes wrong.
steps.action: Reserve a basket of spare contributions for people who come empty-handed.
steps.consequence: They can still take part in the swap.
steps.quote: Set a basket of spare contributions aside for people who turn up empty-handed. A batch that didn't rise shouldn't have to keep a neighbor away.

steps.premise: A child may want to help at the bread table.
steps.action: Invite the child to draw a loaf for display.
steps.consequence: The family can participate together without touching samples.
steps.quote: A child who wants to help could draw a little portrait of a loaf for the table, giving families something to do together without handling the samples.

steps.premise: The closing crew needs to know where leftover contributions can go.
steps.action: Ask bakers in advance to choose a destination for their extra bread.
steps.consequence: The crew can pass it on with each baker's permission.
steps.quote: Invite contributors to choose a home for their spare bread in advance, allowing the closing crew to pass it along with the baker's agreement.

steps.premise: Someone may hesitate to make an imperfect drawing in a public sketchbook.
steps.action: Invite a gardener to put an unfinished pencil sketch near the front.
steps.consequence: Seeing exploratory marks can make a visitor more willing to draw.
steps.quote: Let a gardener contribute an unfinished pencil study near the front. A few searching lines make putting an imperfect mark in a public book feel easier.

steps.premise: A whole garden border can be too much to fit on the page.
steps.action: Offer a small cardboard viewfinder to frame a group of stems.
steps.consequence: The visitor can choose a manageable subject.
steps.quote: A small cardboard viewfinder helps someone faced with a whole border pick a patch of stems that fits on the page.

steps.premise: Another visitor might want to see a drawn plant up close.
steps.action: Leave room beside the drawing for the plant's location.
steps.consequence: The visitor can find the plant in the garden.
steps.quote: Leave space for the plant's garden location beside a drawing, helping another visitor track down an intriguing seed head for a closer look.

steps.premise: Some people want to try a mark privately first.
steps.action: Keep scrap sheets in the pencil tray.
steps.consequence: They can experiment before making a mark in the shared sketchbook.
steps.quote: Keep a few pieces of scrap paper in the pencil tray for people who want to try a mark privately before committing it to the shared book.

steps.premise: Returning visitors may want to see observations from the same month in past years.
steps.action: Shelve completed sketchbooks by season.
steps.consequence: The visitors can find the earlier drawings for that time of year.
steps.quote: Give finished volumes a shelf sorted by season, so a returning visitor can find what other people noticed during the same month in earlier years.

steps.premise: Some visitors like to observe quietly while in company.
steps.action: Occasionally hold a quiet drawing session before a garden tour.
steps.consequence: They can try the shared books with other people in silence.
steps.quote: Offer an occasional quiet drawing period before a garden tour, letting visitors who like to observe in silence try the books in company.

steps.premise: What the performer wears can change how a measured hem will hang.
steps.action: Send each performer a brief list of what to bring or wear for the fitting.
steps.consequence: They can be fitted with the items that affect the costume's fit, such as show shoes.
steps.quote: Send each performer a short list of what to wear or bring, since a trouser hem measured over slippers may sit differently over the show shoes.

steps.premise: Several costume changes can make one performer's fitting run long.
steps.action: Schedule extra time for performers with multiple changes.
steps.consequence: An elaborate costume is less likely to delay the rest of the evening.
steps.quote: Allow a little extra time for people with several changes, so one elaborate costume doesn't quietly push the rest of the evening behind.

steps.premise: Travel delays can leave a fitting slot open.
steps.action: Give performers one named contact to alert about a delay.
steps.consequence: The team can use the gap while there is still time.
steps.quote: Let performers send word to one named contact if their journey is delayed, so the team can fill a gap while there's still time to use it.

steps.premise: The fitter needs to keep time while attending to the performer.
steps.action: Place a legible clock where the fitter can see it.
steps.consequence: They can pace the appointment without frequently looking away.
steps.quote: Keep an easy-to-read clock within the fitter's sight so they can pace an appointment without repeatedly looking away from the performer.

steps.premise: A misunderstood alteration is easy to correct while the costume is being worn.
steps.action: Have the note taker read back the requested alteration before the performer changes.
steps.consequence: The people at the fitting can clarify the request on the spot.
steps.quote: Have the note taker read back the requested change while the costume is still on, when a misunderstood sleeve length takes seconds to put right.

steps.premise: There may be more alterations than the team can finish before some costumes are needed.
steps.action: Record the order of priority the team has agreed on.
steps.consequence: The most urgent work can be addressed in time for rehearsal.
steps.quote: Write down the agreed priorities if there's more sewing than the team can finish, so a costume needed at tomorrow's rehearsal gets attention in time.

steps.premise: Showing a position beside an ongoing match may draw spectators around the players.
steps.action: Put a demonstration board in a corner away from active games.
steps.consequence: A helper has room to teach without crowding someone else's match.
steps.quote: Place a demonstration board in a corner away from active games, giving a helper room to show a position without gathering a crowd around someone else's match.

steps.premise: Visitors may be unsure whether a seated stranger wants to play.
steps.action: Let a seated player turn a sign toward the entrance when they want an opponent.
steps.consequence: Arriving visitors can see whom they may join.
steps.quote: Offer a small sign that a seated player can turn toward the door when they'd welcome an opponent, taking the guesswork out of joining a stranger.

steps.premise: During busy periods people may hover to see which game ends next.
steps.action: Use a written waiting list.
steps.consequence: Visitors can sit and read while they wait.
steps.quote: Keep a written waiting list during busy periods, letting visitors sit down to read instead of hovering over games that look nearly finished.

steps.premise: A missed check may prompt disagreement over undoing a move.
steps.action: Have the two players agree on takebacks before the game starts.
steps.consequence: They can avoid a dispute when someone makes a mistake.
steps.quote: Invite both players to agree before starting whether they'll allow takebacks, heading off a dispute the first time someone overlooks a check.

steps.premise: Animated analysis after a game may continue for a long time.
steps.action: Provide a discussion area away from the quiet boards.
steps.consequence: Players can talk through their finished game without disturbing ongoing play.
steps.quote: Set up a place for post-game discussion a little away from the quiet boards, since a lively analysis can last much longer than the game itself.

steps.premise: A rules disagreement may pull the rest of the room into a dispute.
steps.action: Encourage players to consult the host quietly.
steps.consequence: They can resolve the question without involving the whole room.
steps.quote: Encourage a quiet word with the host if a disagreement develops, giving players a way to settle a rules question without drawing in the whole room.
